books.title: Clean Code
books.author: Robert C. Martin
books.description: A handbook of agile software craftsmanship. It explains how to write code that other people can actually read, name variables so they mean something, and keep functions small enough to understand in one sitting.

books.title: The Pragmatic Programmer
books.author: Andrew Hunt & David Thomas
books.description: Practical advice for working developers, from avoiding duplicated knowledge to automating the boring parts. It treats programming as a craft you keep improving rather than a list of syntax to memorise.

books.title: Refactoring
books.author: Martin Fowler
books.description: A catalogue of small, safe transformations that improve the design of existing code without changing what it does. Each technique is named, described, and shown with a before-and-after example.

books.title: Design Patterns
books.author: Erich Gamma et al.
books.description: The book that named the classic object-oriented patterns such as Observer, Factory and Singleton. It shows the recurring problems each pattern solves and the trade-offs of applying it.

books.title: Introduction to Algorithms
books.author: Thomas H. Cormen
books.description: A rigorous reference covering sorting, graphs, trees, dynamic programming and more. Heavy on proof and analysis, which is why it is the standard text for a data structures and algorithms course.

books.title: Flutter in Action
books.author: Eric Windmill
books.description: A hands-on guide to building cross-platform apps with Flutter and Dart. Covers widgets, state management, layout, and the asset pipeline this very application is built on.

books.title: The Design of Everyday Things
books.author: Don Norman
books.description: Explains why some doors, taps and apps are instantly understandable while others are not. Its ideas about affordances and feedback are the reason modern interfaces look the way they do.

books.title: Dune
books.author: Frank Herbert
books.description: A science fiction novel set on the desert planet Arrakis, where control of the spice trade decides the fate of empires. Included here as the one book in the shelf that is not about software at all.
